Let's talk about something that makes a lot of folks nervous—mistakes, and the fear of getting it wrong, especially when it comes to conversations about race.
You know, talking about race can get really messy. Even people with the best intentions sometimes slip up. Maybe the wrong words come out, or old habits sneak back in right when you least expect them. And honestly, that fear of messing up? It can feel paralyzing. For a lot of us, it’s easier to stay quiet, hoping we won’t say the wrong thing. But here’s the thing—staying silent is its own kind of mistake.
Picture this: someone blurts out a question during a group discussion, only to realize—maybe a second too late—that it was actually pretty insensitive. The room goes quiet. Suddenly, embarrassment hits hard. There’s this desperate urge to explain, to defend, or maybe just to shrink away and hope everyone forgets. Sound familiar? Most of us have been there, stuck between wanting to fix what we just said and just wanting to disappear altogether.
What often gets lost in these moments is a simple truth—mistakes are going to happen. No one has all the right answers, and we’re all shaped by the experiences and ideas we grew up with. The real test isn’t whether you mess up, but how you respond when you do. It’s so tempting to get defensive, to say you “didn’t mean it that way,” or to ask for instant forgiveness. But here’s something important: just because you didn’t mean harm, doesn’t mean there wasn’t any impact.
I remember someone who once apologized for a thoughtless comment, fully expecting things to just go back to normal. Instead, they were met with silence. It was uncomfortable, no doubt about it. But that silence made them sit with what they’d done, rather than rushing to make themselves feel better. Over time, they realized that real growth comes from listening, learning, and making amends—not from seeking quick, easy fixes.
It’s really common to fall into the trap of making these moments about our own guilt or discomfort. But anti-racism work isn’t about being perfect—it’s about being accountable. That means apologizing without making excuses, changing your behavior, and being willing to try again. It also means understanding that trust takes time to rebuild. Some wounds just don’t heal overnight.
So, if you’re feeling that fear of getting it wrong, you’re definitely not alone. But don’t let it stop you from trying. Most people truly appreciate a sincere effort, even if it isn’t flawless. The real key? Approach these conversations with humility, curiosity, and a genuine willingness to learn. Over time, that fear of making mistakes starts to fade, and what grows in its place is a much deeper sense of connection and understanding.
